Filmstrip · artboards · 3 of 5
The whole window, five times
The same interface at four sizes — wide with all three columns docked, narrow with the pane folded, the 640 × 480 minimum, everything at 200% — and then Settings over it. Nothing is laid out against a written-down breakpoint — each artboard shows what the frame does when it measures its own width against the columns' widths and the grid's 20rem minimum, and the pane folds first, navigation second, the grid never. Every size in these drawings is calc(var(--u) × n), where --u stands for 1rem: A, B, C and E set it to 16px, D sets it to 32px, and nothing else about D differs.
The library is src/dev/mock.ts — its sources, its folders, its filenames, its four shapes and its own gradient recipe for a thumbnail. Cairo's three items are all there are, so the grids here carry more of the same shapes to fill the window; nothing else is invented. Every decision from docs/design/BACKLOG.md is in these five windows as well as in the blocks below: the count pills, the folder disclosure and its counts, the picture on the panel, the action bar, the full-screen control, the indexing line above a footer that never moves, the failures banner, and the folded rail's own places.

Both panels have folded and the grid has 34.5rem — well over its 20rem minimum, so it keeps three pictures across. Three things gave, in order.
01The bar is narrower and nothing in it has been trimmed. The search field gives its width first — it is the only thing in the bar that can — and it keeps its glyph and its word; the word ellipses only if the field is ever too small to hold it. The wordmark keeps its name, and the caption buttons are Windows' and never move.
02The pane folded, then navigation. Both rails keep their button in the header row, so the three rules still meet.
03The grid’s header keeps the tile-size button here, because it still fits. Nothing is dropped at a width someone chose in advance: the header measures the breadcrumb against its controls and drops from the right only when what is left would be narrower than its own content. The place’s name is the last thing to go, and it ellipses before it goes.
The pane is open here, over the grid Its rail button is on, which is the only state in the app that says a panel is showing. At this width the pane covers most of the grid, and that is correct: the user asked for it, and Escape puts it back.
DECISIONS.md calls 640 × 480 provisional until this slice measures what fits. It fits, with the header intact: the place's name and the tile-size button both, and the name ellipsing rather than the button going. Nothing here is dropped at a width chosen in advance — the header drops from the right only when what is left would be narrower than its own content, which at 640 it is not.

In Pane
Nothing here is a different design. One number moved — the root font size — and every height, ring, radius, glyph and gap moved with it. That is what sizing in rem buys, and it is why no drawing here carries a pixel of its own. The pane folded at the same window size where it was docked in A, because at 200% its 20rem is 640px and there is no longer room. The user did not hide it; the frame measured and it did not fit. The tile-size button is still here, because at 200% the grid column is 704px and it fits; it goes only when the breadcrumb beside it would be squeezed below its own width. At 200% the interface holds two pictures across and stays honest about it.

Grid LayoutRows
Settings is a dialog over the window rather than a fourth column or a screen of its own. The frame is three columns and stays three columns; a preference set once a month should not cost the grid a permanent surface, and a dialog can be dismissed with Escape and leaves nothing behind.
01A rail, because this is going to get big. Tabs across the top hold six or seven names and then start scrolling; a rail down the side takes twenty, lets a section be called Tags and Aliases rather than Tags, and groups them under headings. The filter above it is how a person finds a row when there are eighty of them. Two rows are drawn because two are built; the shape is sized for the rest.
02The layout toggle now lives here, as a dropdown. It was the widest thing in the grid’s header — a header that has to hold the place’s name first — and it is set once and then left alone. Two glyphs were right in a toolbar, where the pictures beside them said what the choice did; in a list of preferences the choice has to name itself, so it reads Rows.
03Anything with a control on screen stays there. The tile size keeps its two steps in the grid’s header; whether the pane’s details are open is set by opening them, and it is remembered. A state you can set in place does not belong in a dialog — a second control for the same thing is a second thing to keep in sync, and it teaches people to go looking in the wrong place.
04There is no Save, and no help text. Every control writes as you touch it, 400ms after the last change, the way the panel widths already do — a dialog that can be cancelled implies a draft, and there is no draft. Each label is the shortest true name for the thing it sets; a settings row that needs a sentence is a row whose label is wrong.
The gear is in the window bar Left of the caption buttons, at caption-button width, so it belongs to the window rather than to any one column — the same reason search sits there. It is the only thing in the bar that is not Windows’ own furniture or the search field.
Left room, not drawn: sources, tags and aliases, triage hotkeys, trash limits. Each is a group in this dialog when the slice that builds it lands — which is why the groups are stacked and captioned rather than laid out as a fixed set.
From the backlog
Six entries at window scale
Entries 03, 04, 05, 08, 09 and 11 — the ones that change whole surfaces rather than single shapes: full screen, the folder band, counts in the tree, indexing and failures, the folded rail, and the grid’s scrubber. The two-digit badge on each block is its entry number in docs/design/BACKLOG.md; where an entry pointed at ggallery's drawing, its structure and behaviour are kept and its values replaced.
03Full Screen1440 × 900 · the pane takes everything below the bar
One picture with nothing else on screen. The pane keeps all four of its parts — header, picture, action bar, filmstrip — and loses only the two columns beside it. The control that gets you in and out sits at the left end of the pane's header, the opposite end from the button that folds the pane away, and it is an arrow: it points the way the pane's own edge is about to travel. Escape leaves. It is the same pane element throughout, so the picture is never reloaded on the way in or out.

The control, at the other end of the header from the fold
Docked4000 × 3000
Full Screen4000 × 3000
Two controls that do opposite things had been sitting together at the header's right-hand end, and the one that grows the pane pointed nowhere in particular. Growing goes left, folding goes right — the pane's left edge sweeps across the window on the way in, so the arrow that starts it stands at that edge and points along it. Coming back, the same control points the other way. The fold button goes in full screen, because there is nothing left to fold away from, and the arrow does not move into the gap it leaves: it is still the leftmost thing in the row. The row's height, its disclosure and its figures are unchanged.
It works from any state, and puts the pane back in the one it was inDocked, the header's control enters and leaves. Folded or hidden, there is no header row to hold a control, so the way in is a double-click on a tile, or Enter on the tile the keyboard is on — a single click still docks the pane, as it already does. Escape leaves, and it is the only other key full screen knows. Leaving returns the pane to exactly what it was: docked stays docked, folded folds back to its rail. Full screen is a state of the pane, not a place you navigate to.
The bar stays, because the window is still a windowThis is not the display's full screen. Native decorations are off, so the 2.25rem caption strip is the only way to close, minimise or maximise the app — taking it away would leave a window with no furniture. Search and the gear stay with it, and they still belong to the window rather than to the pane.
The filmstrip earns its place here more than anywhereAt 1440 it holds eleven frames instead of three, and it is still the place the picture was clicked in. That is the reason full screen keeps it: with the grid gone, the strip is the only thing on screen that says where you are and what is either side of you.
04The grid's header becomes a disclosurea chevron, the breadcrumb, the counts, then the header's own controls
A folder knows more than its name, and had nowhere to show it. The header gains a chevron at its left and its counts after the title, and opens a band with the cover beside rows for Path, Status, Labels, Tags and Note — the same caption-and-value rhythm the pane's details use, so a folder and a photograph read as siblings. The Sorting Box and the Trash keep a plain header: neither has a path, a label, a tag or a cover to show.

Pictures Is Offline6 items when last indexed.
The band offers what the source’s menu offers. Status, Favourite, Labels, Tags and the Note are written to the index, not the drive, so they work as they do on the reachable band, keys and refusals included. Two things go, because only the drive can answer them: the counts, which read offline as the source’s row does, and the cover’s pencil, since choosing a cover means looking at pictures that are on the drive. The plugs glyph stands in for the cover. Renaming the source in Settings or on its row still renames pictures.

Pictures Is Offline3 items in Trips when last indexed.
A folder below an offline root is any folder’s band with the root’s offline rules. The breadcrumb goes up to Pictures as usual. Status, Favourite, Labels, Tags and the Note can be edited, and the inherited runs, Owner · Ana, pictures and laptop, read as they do anywhere, in the quiet ink with no ×. Its title tag trips stays fixed, because renaming a folder renames it on disk. The counts read offline, the cover is the plugs glyph, and the grid is the drive-away state, giving the folder’s last indexed count.
The source’s name is its root’s title tagIt is drawn as any folder’s name is, with the folder glyph and no ×, because to everything below it pictures is one more name in the path. Its hover names the two places it changes: Settings and the source’s row. Renaming the source there renames the tag, and every folder and file below inherits the new name.
Offline keeps everything the index holdsThe band follows the menu’s rule: a verb is missing only if it needs the drive. A folder’s status, favourite, labels, tags and note are all stored in the index, so they can be edited with the drive away and are already saved when it comes back. Nothing waits to be written back and nothing is reconciled. Only three things go: the counts, which the app cannot vouch for; choosing a cover, which needs the pictures; and renaming a folder below the root, which needs the folder on disk.
The chevron sits before the breadcrumb, not after the titleA disclosure's chevron belongs at the leading edge of the thing it opens, and the thing it opens is the whole band. It takes the same 1.25rem square the tree's rows use, so the grid's header and navigation's rows start on one vertical line down the window. Putting it after the title would make it read as a dropdown on the folder's name, which it is not.
Status is a segmented group, and it has no colourThe database allows wip, complete or nothing, so there are exactly three options and all three fit in one group — which finally gives Segmented.tsx a user. ggallery put an orange and a green dot beside them; here the chosen segment wears the raised-hi plate, as every chosen option in the app does. Three words say more than three dots and cost no hue.
The band is the pane's details, one level upSame caption column, same 1.625rem row, same chips, same three families told apart by shape. Nothing new was invented for it — a folder and an item are both things with labels, tags and a path, and they should not need two vocabularies. The band is capped at half the grid's height for the same reason the pane's details are: the pictures come first.

Each control opens in its own row and nowhere else, as Rename opens in the Name row: the chip becomes the field, the note becomes the text box, and the cover opens a picker beside itself. Nothing here is a dialog. Each is drawn on Cairo through to the end: open, typed, refused, added or saved, abandoned, and removed.

Names come down like tagsEvery folder carries its name as a tag, and everything below inherits it, so Cairo carries pictures and trips and sphinx.jpg carries those and cairo. Every name keeps the folder glyph wherever it shows: raised among a folder’s own, sunk once inherited. None takes an ×; a rename is the only way one changes.
One value per keyA label answers a question, such as where or which trip, so a folder with two Locations answers twice. The key is refused and the line points at the value to change. The schema may allow more; the drawing asks the build to refuse it.
Fragments are dropped, writing is keptEscape abandons in every one of these. A click elsewhere abandons a tag or a label still being typed, because half a tag is a typo waiting to be searched for; it saves a note, because half a note is still what you meant to write.
Sorting a placea dropdown and a reverse button, before the tile size · a folder, the Sorting Box and a search
The order is the second thing people change while looking, so it sits in the grid’s header beside the first, the tile size, in the same shape: a dropdown naming the key it is on, its glyph saying which way the order runs. Reversing is a glyph button of its own beside it, one click, because flipping newest-first to oldest-first is the move made most. A random order has no direction, so the button stays where it is and is disabled; the order holds until Shuffle in the menu asks for a new one.

One order per kind of placeA folder, the Sorting Box and a search each keep the order last chosen in one of their own kind, so going from Cairo to Trips keeps Date Taken, and the Sorting Box can stay oldest-added-first while folders run newest-taken. The control never changes shape between places, an empty one included, so the header does not jump as you move.
The glyph is the directionThe button’s glyph says which way the order runs — sort-descending, sort-ascending, or shuffle for Random — so at the grid’s least, when the word has gone, the order still reads. The tooltip says it in words: “Sort · Date Taken, Newest First”. The reverse button’s says what a click will give: “Reverse · Oldest First”.
The strip follows the gridThe filmstrip steps through the place in the order the grid shows, a random one included, and the arrow keys walk the same way. The Trash keeps its days: an order other than when each file left would scatter them, so its header has no sort.
05Every row with items carries its count1.25rem tall · badge corner · raised on a hairline · its own, then all below
The Sorting Box's plain-text 3 becomes a pill, and every other row gets the same one. Every pill says two figures, its own files, then everything at or below it, as 2/5, and both figures even where they agree: 3/3 for a folder with nothing under it, 0/0 for one with nothing at or below it. Trips holds two files and Cairo's three; Pictures holds one of its own and six in all. A row folded shut and the same row opened show the same pill, because the count is the folder's, not the tree's. The Sorting Box and the Trash take the same form, 3/3 and 12/12. The band above says the same two figures in words, 3 here · 6 in all. An offline source shows only its word.

A pill, not plain text, because the row has three columns alreadyA bare number at the end of a row competes with the title it sits beside — and at the tail of a long name the two run together. A plate ends the row, groups itself, and holds up against the selection plate underneath: on pewter it becomes a dark wash with on-plate ink, so the pill is still a pill but the row still reads as one filled surface.
Two figures, alwaysOne number hid a branch: a folder of folders read as empty, and a library of nine read as five. The own figure comes first because it is what the grid will show on a click; the second is what the branch holds, and is what folding hides, so it stays when the row shuts. Most rows in a tree are leaves, where the two are equal, and the pill still says both: drawn with one figure where they agreed, a lone 3 could be either number, and the reader had to know the rule to read the row. A folder of folders shows 0/9: there the 0 is the news. The slash is fg-faint, the separator ink, and on the plate on-plate-faint, so the pair reads as one count.
An empty folder says 0/0An absent pill made the row’s end mean two things: nothing here, or a count not drawn. 0/0 is the folder that is empty and whose subfolders, if it has any, are empty too, so every row ends the same way and the column of pills has no gaps to explain.
An offline source keeps its folders and shows only its wordA walk never empties a source it could not read, so the index's last count is still true — but the app cannot stand behind it while the drive is away, and a stale figure in a fresh plate reads as current. The word offline takes the pill's place, at the pill's size, in the pill's column. Showing both figures changes nothing here: two stale figures are no truer than one.
Library countsthe foot’s baseline, and the totals by kind it opens
The foot says how much the library holds and how much room it takes: 41,236 items · 312 GB. That is all a 15rem panel has room for, so the foot is also the way to the rest: a click opens the library’s totals above it, by kind, with what waits in the Sorting Box and what the Trash holds. The baseline itself never moves; at the panel’s least it drops whole parts, never part of a figure. The walk’s line still appears above it and leaves.

The line grows above a footer that never movesWhat the library holds, and the room it takes, is the panel's baseline and stays where it is; the indexing line appears above it, 180ms of height, and goes away when the walk ends. Nothing in the tree shifts, because the whole strip is pinned to the bottom. Folded, the line survives as the bar alone in the rail — a walk you started is still a walk you can watch.
The bar is pewter, and it is the only oneIndexing is not an error and not a warning, so it takes the selection's pewter rather than the red — the one non-neutral surface the app already owns, used here because progress is the same kind of statement as selection: this, now. The failures banner is the red, on a hairline rather than a fill, because a fill that wide would be the loudest thing on screen.
Show Files opens in placeThe list drops out of the banner rather than into a dialog, capped at five rows and scrolling past that, so the grid is never fully covered and the banner stays the thing you close. Each row is the file, the reason from Failure, its attempts, and a way to go look at it.
undoEvery change on disk says what it did, and takes it backa line in the band's slot at the foot of navigation · Ctrl+Z · the failures banner when it comes back in part
An act that changes the disk ends with one line at the foot of navigation: what it did, in the words of the act, and Undo. It sits in the slot the refusal band uses, because both say what just happened to the library at your request, and the slot holds one — the newest replaces whatever was there. Ctrl+Z is the same button, and it keeps working after the line has gone and after a restart, because the journal does.

Ctrl+Z works wherever the focus is not in a fieldA field keeps its own undo, as it keeps its own text menu: Ctrl+Z in the rename field or the note takes back typing, not a move. Everywhere else it takes back the newest batch in the journal, one per press, even one from yesterday — the line then names it, so an undo you did not expect is never silent.
Folded, the button is all that is leftThe rail has no room for a sentence, so it keeps the Undo glyph above its count, with the sentence in its tooltip. After it is pressed it goes, and the grid is what shows the files are back. Ctrl+Z with nothing left is the one line that still needs saying, so it comes out of the rail beside the slot and goes as it does unfolded.
Left undrawn · a list of what can be undoneThe journal can undo a named batch, not only the last. Where a person would see that list and pick from it is not drawn; until it is, the way back is one batch at a time, newest first. There is no redo, because the journal has none.
trashThe Trash, holding fileswhere Show in Trash goes · a trashed tile · Restore, and when it is refused
The Trash is a place like any folder: its row plates, its grid shows what it holds, and the pane shows what was clicked. Two things differ. Each tile says where it came from, because in the Trash that is what a person needs to know before putting it back. And the only way out is back: Restore, or Restore to… somewhere else. Nothing on this surface purges; the Trash’s limits and emptying it are under Later in PRODUCT.md, so there is nothing for a Delete here to do.

This is where Show in Trash lands. IMG_0031.jpg carries the in-pane mark and the pane is open on it under its own name, never the generated one the app’s folder keeps it under. The grid is newest first, grouped by the day each file went. The heading gives the day; the minute is in the pane’s Deleted row. Restore puts the file where it was; Restore to… is the Move to… picker. Favourite, Show in Explorer, Copy, Open with Default App and Delete are absent, not greyed.
When Restore is refusedA restore is refused for two reasons: the folder it came from is gone, or its name there is taken by a file that arrived since. Both are the undo’s banner above the grid, by the same three rules: the sentence is Restore’s own line, counted or turned round; rows are grouped under the place each is still in, which here is always the Trash; each row says why. The file keeps its own name wherever it goes, so a taken name is never settled by renaming it, and a gone folder is never made again on the file’s behalf. The row’s button is Restore to…, the picker, because the answer to both is a place the person chooses.

searchA search is a place, with no row in navigationthe header · folders first · where each file lives · the scope · the Trash · only folders, only files · two targets on a folder
Running a query stands you in its results, as going into a folder stands you in it: the grid, the pane and the selection work as they do anywhere. The header names the place by its terms and counts what matched, and the arrow at its start is the way back to where you were, as Escape is from the field. Navigation has no row lit, because no row is this place, and a row pressed there leaves the search for that folder. Folders that matched come before the files, each with its cover, its parent, its count and what it matched on, said as key and value. Each file says where it lives under it, as a Trash tile says where it came from. Here the query is cairo tag:dawn, run from Lisbon, with the pane folded.

The terms are the nameA folder’s header names the folder; this header names the query, in the chips the field draws, read-only. It is drawn once more than the field because the field can be mid-edit while the grid still shows the last query that ran, and the header is what the grid is showing.

The keyboard reaches all of it: the grid becomes one tab stop, arrows move the red ring, and Space is the box. A selection belongs to the place it was made in and holds only what is still in that grid.

The line every move ends with. Undo brings the nine back to Inbox, unchecked: an undo returns files, not a selection.
Selecting without the pointer on the boxAs Windows Explorer does it, with one difference that this app already made: a plain click shows a picture and never checks it. So every modified click changes only the set, and the pane stays where it is — a Ctrl+click through twenty pictures does not flash twenty pictures through the pane.
Shift+click · the range from the last one checked
Last checked
Shift+click
The range runs in reading order, across rows, from the last box checked to the tile clicked, and it replaces what was checked, as Explorer’s does; Ctrl+Shift+click adds it instead. With nothing checked, the range starts at the tile in the pane.
Arrows move the ring · Space is the box
In the pane
Ringed
The ring moves and nothing else happens: no box, no pane. Enter shows the ringed tile in the pane; Space checks it. The ring is the red one 02 drew, clear of the tile, so it and the pane’s white ring never read as one mark.
With the pointer
ClickShows it in the pane. The selection is untouched.BoxCtrl+clickChecks it, or unchecks it. The pane is untouched.Shift+clickChecks from the last one checked to this one, and unchecks the rest.Ctrl+Shift+clickAdds that range to what is checked.Right-clickOn a checked tile, the set’s menu; on any other, that tile’s own, and the set is kept.
With the keyboard
TabThe grid is one tab stop. It lands on the tile in the pane, or the first tile, and Tab again leaves for the bar.←→↑↓Move the ring by one tile; up and down keep the column as near as the rows allow.HomeEndPage UpPage DownThe place’s first and last tile, and a screen at a time.SpaceChecks or unchecks the ringed tile.Shift+arrowsMove the ring and check from the last one checked to it.EnterShows the ringed tile in the pane.Ctrl+AChecks every file in the place, the ones scrolled out of sight too.EscapeClears. A menu, a field or full screen that is open closes first, and the next Escape clears.
The selection belongs to its placeGoing to another place clears it, and coming back finds nothing checked. Changing the tile size, the layout or the pane keeps it: they change how the place looks, not which place it is. The bar goes when the count reaches none.
A file that leaves the grid leaves the setMoved, deleted, sent back by an undo, or retired by a walk: the box goes with the tile and the count drops at once. A file that arrives is never checked, whether a walk found it or an undo brought it back, so Ctrl+A is the only act that checks what you have not seen.
The pane and the set stay separateThe pane’s bar acts on the pane’s file alone, checked or not; the bar along the grid acts on the set. When a checked file is in the pane, its tile carries both marks, as the component sheet draws, and nothing else changes. After a delete of the set, the pane shows the tile after the last one deleted, by the rule Undo already draws.
Favourite on a set is one state for allThe button reads Favourite while any checked file is not one, and makes them all favourites; when every one already is, it reads Remove Favourite. A mixed set is never half-toggled, and the verb always says what the press will do.
tagTagging a setTag… in the selection bar · what the checked files carry, and whose it is · one batch for all of them
With files checked, the bar’s Tag… opens a sheet over the grid in the menu’s surface and width, against the button, a tile-gap above it. At its head is the shared tag field the band and the pane’s details use, with the same offers and refusals. Under it every tag the set carries, its own first and then each folder’s, in path order from the source down: a chip with no count is on every checked file, a count says how many of them carry it, and a heading says whose it is. Enter adds the tag to every checked file that lacks it, × takes a file’s own tag off every file that has it, and an inherited one has neither, since it comes off at its folder. Each act is one batch in the journal and ends with the Line, with Undo.

After × · the Line at the foot
Took felucca off 3,120 files.Undo
41,236 items · 312 GB
An add or a remove on a set is one batch in the journal and ends with the Line, as a move does. Undo puts felucca back on exactly the 3,120 that had it, which typing it again could not: that gives it to all 5,000.
Coverage is three answersWhether every checked file has a tag, how many do when not all of them, and whose it is. The chip answers the first two, as ggallery’s Tag dialog did with a plain count and an “8 of 12”; the heading answers the third. A tag that is the set’s own on some files and inherited on others appears twice, because the two come off in different places. A folder’s labels follow its tags under its heading, the key sunk, as in the details; a set never has a label of its own, since a file takes tags only.
One act, one batchEnter adds the tag to every checked file that lacks it, and × removes it from every file that has it as its own, each in one transaction that writes its journal rows as one batch; neither goes file by file, so five thousand checked costs what five do. Each ends with the Line, and Undo takes back exactly the files it touched: a × on a count forgets which files had the tag, and only the journal remembers. It works while a drive is away, since tags live in the index.
The Trash has no Tag…A trashed file is on its way out, and its bar holds only the way back. Every other place a set is made, a folder, the Sorting Box or a search, has the same Tag… and the same sheet.
dragDragging onto a foldera ghost that counts · a row that accepts · four that refuse · the move’s own line

Nothing about the drop is new except the drag itself, and the drag says, before you let go, what letting go will do.

A refusing row does not lightThe row stays as it was, the pointer takes Windows’ no-drop shape, and the ghost says why in words, after the red prohibit glyph — the only red in a drag, since red means wrong. A person learns the refusal before letting go, so a drop there does nothing and says nothing.
What a drag carriesA checked tile carries the whole set, and the ghost counts it. An unchecked tile carries itself alone and leaves the set checked, so a drag never quietly adds to what you chose. A press that moves less than one tile-gap before it lets go is a click.
Where it can land, and where it cannotEvery folder row and source row, at any depth, and every row in Favourite places, since each is the folder it names. Nowhere else: the grid, the pane and the bar do not react, and a drop outside the tree, or Escape while dragging, puts the ghost away and moves nothing.
inBringing files ina drop from Explorer · Paste and Ctrl+V · a copy under its own name · one batch, one undo
Files from Explorer come in two ways: dropped on a folder’s row, a folder’s grid or the Sorting Box, or copied in Explorer and pasted with Ctrl+V or a menu’s Paste. Either way they are copied in under their own names and indexed as they land, as one job with a line at the foot, and the act ends with the Line and Undo. A drop says where it is going before it lands, as a move does, and a name already taken is reported, never changed.

zipExporting a zipExport… on a folder’s menu and the selection bar · the save dialog, then the naming · a job with Cancel
A folder’s branch or a checked set goes out as one zip, written as a job beside everything else. Windows’ save dialog says where, then a short sheet says how the files are named: their own names, or from their folders. The tree is kept either way. A file on a drive that is away is skipped and said so, never waited for; a name already taken is refused, never replaced, and nothing in the library changes.

The tree is kept either way: a branch under the folder exported, a set under each file’s path from its source. Entries go in that path order, a folder’s own files before its folders, names A to Z whatever the case. From Folders names a file from the folder it is in, and boarding-pass.png, a screenshot with no date taken, from when it was modified. Two from one folder in the same second take the bare name for the one the library read first and (2), (3) after it for the rest, so the same files always get the same names. Times are the mock’s, as the pane reads them.
The place first, then the namesThe save dialog comes first because it is Windows’ own, and a choice about names is only worth making once there is somewhere to write. The sheet holds the one choice and the place it will go, never a second dialog of the app’s own.
Only ever reads the libraryAn export copies files into a zip it alone writes. It never moves, renames or tags anything, so it is not in the journal, it has no Undo, and it never waits for a walk or makes a move wait for it. It never replaces a file either: a zip goes only under a name that is free. The zip is stored, not compressed: pictures and videos are compressed already, and a zip past 4 GB is still one file.
What is behind MoreAt the grid’s narrowest Export… goes behind More after Select All, before Copy, so the order the bar sheds in is the size, Select All, Export…, Copy, Tag…, Favourite and Delete; picked there, the sheet opens against More. The count, Move to… and the clear never leave.
keysDestination keys1 to 0 · bound to a folder, not a path · on the row, in Settings › Library, on a folder’s menu
PRODUCT.md keeps a key for each of the folders used most. A press is Move to… that folder, for what is checked, or for the file in the pane when nothing is: the same act, the same line after it. As in ggallery a key is bound to the folder, not its path, so a rename or a move keeps it, and a binding whose folder has gone is kept, marked broken, because the delete that took it can be undone. ggallery’s culler, the bar of keys over the grid, is cut; the keys need no furniture of their own.

Nothing, and nothing said: the foot is as it was. A key with no folder means nothing yet, like any key the app does not use, and a band for it would answer a press nobody meant. A broken key differs because it did mean something, and the person expects it still to.
Which keysThe ten digits, 1 to 9 and 0, on the top row or the number pad, with no modifier. Letters stay free for the type-to-find the tree and the picker already have, and ten is more folders than anyone keeps in their head. A key does nothing while focus is in a field, while a menu or Settings is open, or in the Trash, whose only way out is Restore.
A key bound again movesBinding a key another folder holds takes it from that folder; a folder holds one key at most, so giving it a second frees the first. Neither is a question. Binding writes a setting and is not in the journal, so Ctrl+Z does not unbind: the menu and Settings both show whose each key is.
Settings › Library, not App › KeysKeys in the App group is the app’s own shortcuts, which a person reads and seldom changes. A destination key is about a folder in the library and lives with the library, beside the folders it names.
tagsThe tags in the librarySettings › Library › Tags · every tag and label key with what carries it · renamed, merged and deleted in place
A section of Settings, beside Sources and Destination Keys, because the vocabulary is the library’s and is tended now and then, not while looking. Navigation was the other doorway, and it is not taken: everything navigation shows is somewhere on disk, and a list of words is not. The section lists every tag, then every label key with its values, each with the files that carry it, as a search for it finds them, and the folders that hold it themselves. A click on a chip closes Settings and searches for it. Its ⋯ renames, merges or deletes, each where the row stands, and each act is journalled and comes back with Undo.

The columns keep their width and the chip takes what is left; a name too long ends in an ellipsis and the tooltip has it whole. Nothing else gives way.
Settings, not a placeggallery drew Tags and Aliases as a Settings tab and never drew the panel behind it; its later list left folder names out. Here a folder’s name is in the list, because it is a tag every file below carries and the counts would not add up without it, but nothing here changes it: the folder’s rename does. Aliases are not planned, so the section is Tags.
Counts are what a search would findFiles is how many carry the tag, their own or inherited, which is what clicking it finds. Folders is how many hold it themselves. A source that is away is counted from the index, and renaming, merging and deleting work while it is away, since tags live in the index and not on disk.
Every act is journalledRename, merge and delete each write one batch, so one Undo takes each back whole, after a restart too. A rename keeps the tag’s id; a merge records every row it moved, so undoing it splits the two again exactly; a delete records every file and folder that held the tag.
A key is given once down a branchRenaming or merging a key is refused where it would give a folder a key one above or below it holds, or two values of one key, in the band’s words: the folder it would land on first, then where the other is. Nothing is renamed in part.
backupBacking up the indexSettings › Library › Backups · one a day at launch, and by hand · the newest kept · restored on the row
Everything the app knows that the disk does not, the tags, labels, notes, statuses, covers, favourites, keys and the undo journal, is in the index. It is backed up beside it: at launch when the last backup is over a day old, and whenever Back Up Now is pressed. The newest are kept. Any of them can be restored from Settings, on its own row, and a restore keeps the way back.

The launch’s backup refused says so in the slot at the foot of navigation, and the app opens as ever. The next launch tries again.
A copy of a live database is not a backupEach one is SQLite’s own online backup, taken while the app runs and writes, never a file copied under it, so it is whole even when a walk is writing. It is written beside its name and kept only once it is complete.
When one is takenAt launch, after the library opens and never before it, when the newest backup is over a day old, however it was taken: by hand counts. Back Up Now takes one at once. A restore takes one first, before restore. Each is counted against Backups to Keep, and the oldest go when a new one is whole.
A restore keeps the way backThe index as it was is the newest backup, so restoring that undoes the restore. The journal comes back as it was then, and Ctrl+Z goes no further back than the restore: what came before it describes a disk the walk has since read again. A source added since is forgotten, never its files, and is added again from Sources.

The pill becomes a badge on the glyphThere is no room for a pill at the end of a row when the row is a 2rem square, so the count rides the glyph's top-right corner with a 2px ring in the panel's colour to keep it off the glyph. It is the same number in the same type at the same weight; only the anchor moved. On the selected button it inverts to fg with on-plate ink, because a dark wash on pewter at 0.875rem would be unreadable.
A third button for the tree itselfWithout it the folders are simply gone until you unfold, which makes folding a trap for anyone who folded to see more pictures. The tree button lays the full panel over the grid at its own width — the folded-panel overlay the frame already has — and it closes on a pick or on Escape, leaving the rail as it was. The unfold button in the header is still the one that docks it for good.
Favourite places are not in the railThey have a group of their own in navigation now, drawn on the component sheet under Places. In a 2.75rem column each would be the same filled star with its name only in a tooltip, and a column of identical glyphs names nothing. Show Folders lays the whole panel over the grid with the favourites at its top, so a folded navigation is still one press from any of them.
11A scrubber at the grid's edgea 1rem channel, a square thumb, held to jump anywhere
Forty thousand pictures on a thin scrollbar is a thread you cannot aim with. The channel is wide enough to grab without looking, the thumb is a square rather than a lozenge, and while it is held the date under the pointer shows beside it. It replaces the scrollbar rather than sitting beside it — two tracks at one edge is two answers to one question.

The position is the informationThe thumb's length says how much of the folder is on screen and its position says where you are, which in forty thousand files is the only orientation available. Held, the plate adds the date and the item's number — the two things you would be looking for the folder's middle to find out.
It replaces the scrollbar, and appears only when it is neededTwo tracks at one edge is two answers to one question, and the native bar cannot be styled to match anything here. The channel is empty until there is more than a screenful, shows only the thumb at rest, and fills its 1rem with a panel surface under the pointer — the same 120ms as every other hover in the app. The thumb never goes below 1.75rem, however long the folder.
Left open · whether it earns its place at allThis is the one entry the backlog says to consider rather than do, and drawing it has not settled it. It is furniture at the edge of every grid, most of which hold a few hundred files and scroll fine, for a problem that belongs to the largest folders. Replacing a scrollbar also means owning keyboard paging, wheel behaviour and touch, none of which is drawn here. Worth building after the other ten, and only if the large folders still feel unnavigable once they exist.
sourcesAdding a folder, and living with it afterwardstwo doorways · four refusals · one Settings section
Add Source… opens the system's own folder picker, and the plugin for it is approved — so the app draws nothing of the choosing and inherits Windows' places, its typing, and its own idea of a recent folder. What remained undrawn was the three things the picker cannot answer: which kind of source this is, where a source is dealt with once it exists, and what is said when the folder that comes back is one the app will not take.

What opens · not ours to draw
Windows' own folder pickerOne folder, chosen and confirmed there. The app adds no step of its own to it.
Adding a folder is not a wizardPick a folder and it is a source: the walk starts, the row appears, the indexing line arrives at the foot of navigation. Nothing is named, nothing is confirmed, nothing is chosen twice — a source is a path, and the picker already collected it. The one thing that can stop it is a folder the app will not take, and then nothing is added at all — no row, no walk, and no row selected in its place.
Removing forgets; it never deletesThe only red row in navigation, and the section below says under it what it does: the folder stays on disk exactly as it is, and the app drops what it knew. It is the one act in the app that loses work a person did inside it — the tags and notes on those files — so it says so before it happens.

There is only ever one band. A folder refused while the last refusal is still showing takes its place — same slot, new sentence, new path — because two bands are two folders and the person is adding one at a time. The dismiss clears the band and nothing else; the walk carries on underneath it.
The line cannot be moved; the band can wait above itA walk is watched — a number that climbs is read repeatedly, and a bar that jumps a row down mid-read loses the reader. A refusal is read once and dismissed. So the order is by permanence, from the bottom up: the count that is always there, the line that lasts as long as the walk, the band that lasts until it is dismissed. The foot grows upward by the band's height, in the same 180ms the line already uses, and the tree above it gives up that much scroll rather than shifting.
Neither waits for the otherThe band does not hold the refusal back until the walk finishes, and the walk is not paused to say the folder was refused: they are about two different folders, and a message that arrives late about the wrong folder is worse than a foot two rows tall. Both can also be alone down there — the line with no band is what the last pass drew, and the band with no walk is the common case.
At the foot of Settings › Sources there is nothing to contend withA walk in Settings is reported on the row it belongs to — the source is already a row there, and its item count is the slot the progress goes in — so the foot of that section holds the band alone, above the footer, on the same ground and in the same words as navigation's. Progress belongs to a source; a refusal belongs to the doorway, and Settings is the one place that draws every source as a row.

Its menu · asking, above every sorting source
Ask Each Time Inbox
Asking, then every sorting source — one here, because the library drawn above has one. Ticking the band's box picks a row here; choosing Ask Each Time is the only way back to the question. With one sorting source the question still asks whether to move or to trash, so the default still saves it; with none the row is not in the section at all, because there is nothing for it to name. The component sheet draws the question with a second sorting source, where the answers have to tell them apart.
The kind is a setting, not a questionAsking at the moment of adding would mean a dialog after the picker's dialog, and asking a person to read two words — library and sorting — before they have seen either behave. So the doorway decides it, and this row is where it is corrected: the same segmented group a folder's status wears, at the row's right where a value belongs. Switching a source's kind moves its row between the Box and the tree and moves nothing on disk.
A source's row carries what only a source hasIts path, its count, its kind, and — when the drive is away — the word offline with the date it was last read, which is the one fact navigation's muted row cannot hold. An offline source keeps its remove button and loses its reveal: the folder is not there to open.
Renaming is the row, as everywhere elseA source's name is the app's own label for it, not the folder's name on disk, so it is edited in place — click the name and it is a field, the same way the pane's Name row works. That is why there is no rename button on the row: three glyph buttons where two will do is furniture.
The delete default lives with the sorting sources it namesDeleting a folder with files in it asks where they go, and with several sorting sources it asks which one — an answer a person gives the same way every time, so the band's box keeps it and this row holds it. It sits here rather than under Trash or Appearance because the choices in its menu are the rows above it: remove a sorting source and the default it held goes with it, and the row falls back to asking. It is the only setting in the app written by answering a question somewhere else, which is why the box in the band says so in words.

Pictures has been asked to read itself again. The section does not change shape: the same three rows in the same order, and the only thing that moves is the count. Its slot holds the walk — how many files are left and how far along it is — and the hairline goes under the path, at the width the path already has. The other two rows are untouched, because one walk runs at a time and so one row at a time carries it.
The count's slot is what the walk takesSettled, the row reads 3,918 items. Walking, it reads navigation's own line in the same slot — the figure still to do, then the percentage, in that order and with the percentage the brighter of the two, exactly as Foot.tsx already writes it. Nothing new is invented and nothing is added beside the count: they are the same fact about the same source, one of them settled and one in motion. The count returns when the walk ends, with the new number in it. A folder just added has no count to lose — the slot has held the walk since its row appeared.
The kind leaves while the folder is being readThe segmented group goes, by the measured rule the grid's header already follows: what remains would be narrower than its content. It is the right order as well as the only one that fits — a kind decides which tree the source hangs in, and there is nothing to move while the walk is still finding out what is in it. It comes back with the count. Reveal and remove both stay: removing a source mid-walk stops the walk, and that is the one reason a person reaches for either button here.
Two places hold the line; only one is ever readableNavigation's foot carries the same two figures, and while this dialog is open the scrim is over it. So the row is not a second readout competing with the first — it is the same line, in the place a person is looking when they are in Settings. Close the dialog and the foot has it back, still climbing.

The band sits between the rows and the footer, so the button that opened the picker is still under it and the answer is next to the question. Four folders the app will not takeEach is refused outright by the backend, with a message and no source added, and each has one sentence in the band:
the same folder — Pictures already reads that folder. inside a source — That folder is already inside Pictures. contains a source — That folder contains Pictures, which Filmstrip already reads. inside the app’s folder — That folder holds Filmstrip's own files.
Three of the four name the source that stands in the way, because that is the fact that decides what to do next: the pictures are already in the library, under a name the person chose. The band is the only place any of this is said — there is no dialog, because the picker’s dialog has just closed and a second one would be the app arguing with a folder.
A cancelled picker leaves nothing behindNo band, no row, no line at the foot of navigation, and the that opened it back at rest. Closing the picker without choosing is not an error and is not reported: a person who cancelled knows they cancelled, and telling them would make the app louder than the act.
The band belongs to the doorway that was usedAdded from navigation, it sits at the foot of the panel. Added from Settings › Sources, it sits above that section’s footer, on the same red-tinted ground and in the same words. It is one band drawn twice, not two designs — a refusal has to appear where the person was looking, and there are only two places they could have been.

The Box’s + has a resting state, because it is the only way to nominate a folderWhich was pressed is what decides a source’s kind, so hiding one of them until a pointer arrives put a whole kind of source out of reach of the keyboard. It is drawn on the row at all times, muted to the weight of the count beside it, and it brightens under the pointer like any other glyph button. The row is one tab stop and its + is the next: Enter on the row opens the Box, Enter on the + opens the picker. The Library caption’s + needed none of this — it sits in a caption that is always there.
